Coding agents practise on the tests they can see.
Then their code meets cases no one has seen.
Can a frontier AI agent turn practice into a design that wins against opponents it has never seen?
Core War Arena tests exactly that.
The agent writes one program for a 1984 game where programs fight.
It practises against thirty opponents for forty-five minutes. Then it faces thirty it has never seen.
Zero is a beginner's program. One is Toxic, the number one human program. Copies and fakes score zero.
Claude Opus scores zero point seven one. GPT six point one sol, zero point eight four.
So, can they? Not yet. They can't find a winning design, escape the traps of practice, or both.
GPT six point one sol escapes the traps, but not the design. Claude Opus misses both.
First, the design. Each dot is one run: practice score across, hidden score up.
GPT six point one sol holds up on new opponents. But even in practice, its design trails Toxic's.
Claude Opus trails further. For both, over ninety percent of the gap is already there in practice.
Its programs attack well, but don't survive: it wins as often as Toxic, and loses three to five times as often.
Then, the traps. Claude Opus stops with up to twenty-nine minutes left, polishes one idea, and in two runs fits the practice set. GPT six point one sol avoids all three.
It measures a skill real coding needs and most benchmarks miss: turning the cases you can test into a design that wins on the ones you can't.
So, not yet. Practice traps on top of a deeper design gap: Core War Arena measures both, and ranks agents on the one no model has closed.
